message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
The arithmetic in the document is correct as far as it goes, and the competitor check supports the new prices. But the projection leaves out the beef cost rise that the paper itself reports, the case for removing the risotto is the reverse of what Table 1 shows, and the package as a whole lowers the main-course margin instead of lifting it to 71%. The changes may still be worth making, but they aren't as well evidenced as your summary says.

## What checks out

- **Table 1 is internally consistent.** Every margin matches price and food cost, and the plates add up to the stated 1,050 a week.
- **The headline arithmetic is right.** 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2 = £810 a week, and × 52 = £42,120.
- **The prices stay below the competitor midpoints.** The midpoints are £17.98 for fish, £16.50 for burgers and £29.50 for steak, so £17.50, £16.00 and £28.00 are all below them.

## 1. The 12% beef rise is left out of the projection

Section 4 says beef prices rise 12% on the same day the new prices take effect, but section 5.3 counts only the extra revenue.

| | Extra food cost per plate | Plates per week | Extra cost per week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger (£4.20 → £4.70) | £0.50 | 260 | £131 |
| Steak (£10.40 → £11.65) | £1.25 | 120 | £150 |
| **Total** | | | **£281** |

The net gain from the price rises is about **£529 a week, or £27,500 a year**, not £42,000. Even after the increases, both beef dishes earn a lower percentage margin than today:
- burger: 72% → 70.6%
- steak: 60% → 58.4%

## 2. The risotto has the *best* margin, not the weakest

From Table 1, the risotto's margin is **80%, the highest on the menu**. In cash terms it makes £11.20 a plate, more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90). Its 90 plates a week tie with the specials for lowest sales, so it isn't the lowest outright.

The proposed replacement makes the problem worse. Specials currently average a 64% margin. If the new vegetarian special matches that at £14, its food cost is about £5.04 a plate against the risotto's £2.80. That costs roughly **£200 a week** in gross profit, assuming volumes stay the same. Its actual cost isn't known yet, but nothing in the paper suggests the swap improves margin.

There may be good reasons to change the risotto, such as menu freshness, kitchen workload or customer feedback. The paper should argue it on those grounds, because the data point the other way.

## 3. The 71% margin doesn't hold up

Using the five named dishes (the specials' prices aren't given):

| Scenario | Main-course margin | Change in gross profit per week |
|---|---|---|
| Current | 69.9% | baseline |
| Price rises only, as in the paper | 71.3% | +£810 |
| + beef cost rise | 69.7% | +£529 |
| + risotto replaced by a 64% special | 68.5% | +£328 |

With every effect included, gross profit rises by about **£17,000 a year**, but margin *falls* by more than a point. The proposal won't help restore the 70% target as claimed.

## 4. Other issues

- **"Six trading days":** section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days.
- **"Remain the value option":** today we're the cheapest in the group for all three dishes. After the increases we're cheaper than the midpoint but no longer the cheapest for any of them. That's a reasonable position, but the paper should say so plainly.
- **Repeat guests aren't proof of price tolerance.** A 60% repeat rate shows loyalty, but frequent diners are also the people most likely to notice a £1–2 rise. The 2024 increase having "no visible effect" is the stronger evidence, and the paper should give the actual booking or cover figures from before and after it.
- **The monitoring can't detect the effect it's meant to.** Comparing April–May sales with a January–February baseline mixes the price effect with seasonal change, since spring trade normally differs from winter. It would be better to compare with April–May 2025, or to track each dish's share of total mains. The paper should also set a trigger in advance, for example "if fish and chips falls more than 8% year on year, review."
- **No sensitivity check.** Against the higher beef costs, the new prices break even if volume falls by about 8% for fish and chips, 9% for burgers and 12% for steak. That's a useful cushion, and including it would strengthen the case.

## Suggested changes before it goes to the owners

1. Restate the projection net of the beef increase: about £27,500 a year from the price rises.
2. Either drop the risotto proposal or argue it on non-margin grounds. Set a food-cost target for the replacement, for example ≤ £2.80 to protect the 80% margin.
3. Correct the 71% claim and "six trading days."
4. Consider whether the burger and steak need a little more, since even after the rises they lose margin against beef costs. The steak could go to £29, still under the £29.50 midpoint.
5. Use a year-on-year comparison for monitoring, with a stated review trigger.

The price increases themselves look sensible and defensible. The main fixes are presenting the projection honestly and reversing the reasoning on the risotto.
